item.title: Fatal Opioid-Like Toxidrome Associated With a 7-Hydroxymitragynine Kratom Product.
item.description:
Ann Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Gerona R, Ellison R, Conners R et al.

Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) use has increased in the United States, with the market shifting from traditional leaf preparations to concentrated products containing concentrated or chemically processed alkaloids such as 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl. These formulations may deliver supraphysiologic opioid-receptor agonist doses with poorly characterized toxicity. A 42-year-old man was found dead at home after reportedly ingesting 3 tablets of a commercial "7-HMG" product and several beers. Postmortem examination revealed purge fluid at the mouth and nose, severe bilateral pulmonary edema, distended bladder, and no evidence of trauma or injection drug use. Quantitative analysis of the remaining tablet showed 29 mg 7-HMG and 0.58 mg mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, with minimal mitragynine. Postmortem blood contained 37.3 ng/mL 7-HMG and 76 ng/mL mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, whereas gabapentin and other medications were present at subtherapeutic concentrations. Compared with an estimated 1 to 4.5 mg 7-HMG in a typical high dose of dried kratom leaf powder, this ingestion delivered approximately 87 mg 7-HMG (19-fold to 87-fold greater 7-HMG exposure than a high-dose botanical leaf preparation). Given the high μ-opioid receptor activity of 7-HMG and its in vivo conversion to the even more potent opioid agonist mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, the postmortem findings are most consistent with a fatal opioid-like toxidrome associated with exposure to concentrated kratom alkaloids. This case illustrates the emerging risk posed by new kratom-branded products containing purified or chemically enriched alkaloids at doses far exceeding traditional preparations.

item.title: Associations Between Diagnostic Blood-Based Biomarkers and Neuroimaging Findings in Mild Traumatic Brain Injury.
item.description:
Ann Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI, TBI] [strong match]
Pandey S, Chen Y, Yue JK et al.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a prevalent and resource-intensive injury in the emergency department (ED). The blood-based biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin c-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) have demonstrated diagnostic potential for acute structural brain injury. Our objective was to clinically validate a US Food and Drug Administration-approved plasma test to aid in the identification of intracranial injury in patients with mTBI presenting to the ED and assess its integration with existing protocols.

METHODS: This single-center validation study enrolled 104 adult patients with suspected mTBI undergoing head computed tomography (CT) for evaluation between October 2023 and June 2024 at a Level I trauma center. Peripheral blood draw was completed within 12 hours postinjury and processed at the hospital clinical laboratory. Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values for the test were calculated and compared with a standard clinical decision rule (Canadian Head CT Rule). ED length of stay and diagnostic turnaround times were examined.

RESULTS: Within the cohort (n=104), 83 patients had elevated biomarker levels (GFAP >30 pg/mL or UCH-L1 >360 pg/mL), and 11 patients had intracranial injury identified on CT. The combination plasma test demonstrated high sensitivity (0.91 [95% confidence interval {CI} 0.59 to 1.00]) but low specificity (0.22 [95% CI 0.14 to 0.31]) for predicting intracranial injury on CT with low positive predictive value (0.12 [95% CI 0.06 to 0.21]) and high negative predictive value (0.95 [95% CI 0.76 to 1.00]). These findings are consistent with prior studies (pooled sensitivity 0.97 [95% CI 0.95 to 0.98]; specificity 0.28 [95% CI 0.23 to 0.34]). False-positive cases (78%) were older than true-negative cases (median 72 years [interquartile range (IQR) 54 to 83] versus 58.5 years [IQR 38.25 to 66]). Median turnaround time for the GFAP/UCH-L1 test was 2 hours faster than head CT (1.09 hours [IQR 0.87 to 1.65] versus 3.28 hours [IQR 2.37 to 4.70]).

CONCLUSIONS: Blood biomarkers for mTBI have potential as an initial rule-out tool for intracranial injury prior to obtaining CT imaging; however, large multicenter studies are needed to clarify its impact on ED resource utilization, length of stay, and acute and long-term costs and benefits to patients and health care systems.

item.title: Micromobility Injury Patterns and Resource Use in US Trauma Centers.
item.description:
J Am Coll Surg | Tier 2 Filtered [Facial/Neck, General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Abbasi B, Chu PW, Carlisle MN et al.

BACKGROUND: Micromobility-related injuries increasingly contribute to trauma care, but differences in injury patterns and resource use across bicycle, e-bike, and e-scooter injuries remain incompletely characterized. We compared injury severity, injury patterns, and resource use among injured riders presenting to participating trauma centers.

STUDY DESIGN: We queried the American College of Surgeons National Trauma Data Bank (2023-2024) for injured bicycle, e-bike, and e-scooter riders ≥18 years. The primary outcome was severe injury (Injury Severity Score ≥16). Secondary outcomes included serious regional injuries (Abbreviated Injury Scale ≥3), craniofacial fractures, operative and critical care resource use, and in-hospital mortality.

RESULTS: Among 47,102 injured riders, 32,100 (68%) rode bicycles, 8,744 (19%) e-bikes, and 6,258 (13%) e-scooters. Compared with bicycle riders, e-scooter riders had lower risk of severe injury (aRR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87-0.99) but higher risk of serious head/neck injury (aRR 1.10, 95% CI 1.04-1.17). Risks of serious chest (aRR 0.77, 95% CI 0.71-0.82) and extremities/pelvic girdle injuries (aRR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.99), emergency surgery (aRR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50-0.87), early transfusion (aRR 0.71, 95% CI 0.54-0.94), and in-hospital mortality (aRR 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.94) were lower. Helmet use was associated with lower craniofacial fracture risk, most strongly among e-scooter riders (aRR 0.49, 95% CI 0.41-0.58).

CONCLUSIONS: Among injured riders presenting to participating trauma centers, e-scooter injuries were associated with lower overall severity and resource use than bicycle injuries but greater serious head/neck injury risk. Helmet use was associated with lower craniofacial fracture risk, supporting continued helmet promotion.

item.title: Prehospital Analgesia in Trauma: A Systematic Review of Current Evidence.
item.description:
Emerg Med Australas | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Prehospital] [strong match]
Alkoby-Meshulam L, Shahar C, Jacob R et al.

OBJECTIVES: Pain management is integral to prehospital trauma care. However, due to multiple challenges, pain is frequently undertreated despite important physiologic and psychologic implications. Among these challenges is uncertainty regarding the safety and effectiveness of pharmacologic agents administered enroute. We aimed to evaluate the level of evidence for the safety and effectiveness of prehospital pharmacologic analgesia for acutely injured adult trauma patients.

METHODS: An electronic database search of PUBMED, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, Embase and Scopus for studies that reported on safety and/or effectiveness of prehospital pharmacologic analgesia for acutely injured adults (aged > 15 years) from January 1st, 2014, to January 1st, 2026. Non-original studies, paediatric studies, studies of non-pharmacologic agents or non-systemic administration (e.g., topical) were excluded.

RESULTS: Seventeen studies, involving 17,115 patients, met the inclusion criteria. The studies consisted of 6 randomized controlled trials, 5 retrospective cohort studies, one retrospective comparative study, one retrospective observational study, two prospective observational studies, one prospective cohort study and one non-randomized clinical trial. Agents included opioids, ketamine, methoxyflurane and paracetamol. Apart from one study of opioid therapy, no drug-attributed serious adverse events were reported. Minor adverse effects such as nausea, dizziness, dysphoria, agitation and drowsiness were common. All agents demonstrated effectiveness to varying levels.

CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence demonstrates an overall favourable safety and effectiveness profile of prehospital analgesia for adult trauma patients. However, considering the wide prehospital prevalence of injury-related pain, evidence is limited by scope, methodology and variations of treatment protocols.

item.title: Association between transfer pathways and functional outcomes in severe trauma patients: a cohort study using the PATOS registry.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Nakagawa K, Sagisaka R, Morioka D et al.

OBJECTIVE: Optimal transport strategies for severe trauma remain debated, particularly in Asia. We evaluated the association between interhospital transfer and functional outcome and its consistency across Asian trauma systems.

METHODS: This cohort study used the Pan-Asian Trauma Outcome Study (PATOS) registry. We analyzed patients with severe trauma (Injury Severity Score > 15) in South Korea, Malaysia, and Vietnam (2015-2022). The exposure was interhospital transfer (Transfer) versus direct transport to a definitive-care hospital (Direct). The primary outcome was a favorable functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale ≤3). The primary model was a country fixed-effect logistic regression estimating the total effect; country-specific estimates and a transport-pathway × country interaction were pre-specified.

RESULTS: Of 9857 patients (Direct, n = 6725; Transfer, n = 3132; 89.2% of transfers in South Korea), a favorable functional outcome occurred in 4701/6403 (73.4%) versus 1830/2991 (61.2%). Transfer was associated with lower odds overall (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.78-0.95), but estimates differed by country (South Korea 1.06, 0.95-1.18; Malaysia 0.53, 0.36-0.80; Vietnam 0.17, 0.11-0.25; interaction P < 0.001; I

CONCLUSION: Interhospital transfer was associated with a lower likelihood of a favorable functional outcome, but this was not uniform across the three trauma systems and was dominated by Korean data, in which no association was observed. These findings require confirmation in analyses anchored at injury or first medical contact.

item.title: Injury patterns and early operative demand in a combined military and civilian casualty cohort: A single-centre study from the first 11 weeks of the 2023 Israel-Hamas war.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [weak match]
Sasson I, Chaushu H, Ungar OJ

INTRODUCTION: Modern asymmetric warfare and large-scale terror attacks produce distinctive wounding patterns that differ from conventional state-on-state conflict and impose specific early demands on receiving trauma systems. The 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel and the ensuing war generated a compressed surge of combined civilian and military casualties. We characterized injury patterns and linked them to early in-hospital resource use at a single tertiary trauma centre across the opening weeks of the conflict.

METHODS: We performed a retrospective descriptive cohort study of 192 consecutive trauma casualties admitted between 7 October and 24 December 2023. Demographics, mechanism of injury, injured anatomical regions, Injury Severity Score (ISS) and acute interventions were abstracted from the institutional trauma dataset. Mechanism and anatomical categories were not mutually exclusive. Variables were summarised as medians (IQR) or counts (percentages); missing data were not imputed and percentages were computed over non-missing observations.

RESULTS: Casualties were young (median age 24 years, IQR 21-35) and predominantly male (84.4%). Penetrating (43.2%) and shrapnel (31.2%) mechanisms predominated, followed by acoustic trauma (12.0%). Extremities were most often injured (lower limb 41.7%, upper limb 35.4%); 68.8% had at least one extremity injury and 37.0% had two or more injured regions. Median ISS was 9 (IQR 4-16); 26.5% of those with a recorded ISS had ISS ≥16. Blast and crush carried the highest median ISS (25 and 16). Early resource use was substantial: 23.4% required emergency surgery via direct emergency-room-to-operating-room transfer, 10.9% mechanical ventilation and 5.2% packed red-cell transfusion.

CONCLUSIONS: This extremity-predominant, penetrating-and-shrapnel profile, with a small but disproportionately severe blast and crush subgroup and frequent acoustic trauma, translated into early demand for emergency surgery, ventilation and transfusion. These patterns support resourcing limb-salvage and damage-control surgery, blood-bank and intensive-care readiness, and audiologic follow-up in military and mass-casualty trauma planning.

Full text via DOI

item.title: Prehospital factors associated with calcium derangements upon arrival to the trauma center from scene - A subanalysis of a multicenter prospective study.
item.description:
Am J Emerg Med | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Haemorrhage, Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Schauer SG, Nicholson SE, Rizzo JA et al.

BACKGROUND: Existing data suggests that hypocalcemia may be a factor in the lethal diamond of trauma. This could offer a potential opportunity for prehospital interventions to address these derangements. We performed a preplanned secondary analysis of data from a prospective multicenter study on calcium derangements in hemorrhage patients upon arrival at trauma centers.

METHODS: We conducted a prospective multicenter observational study of trauma patients admitted at the highest level of activation for three participating centers where an ionized calcium level was measured upon arrival. Data from the prehospital records were collected from the Emergency Medical Services reports. We compared study variables between patients who were hypocalcemic, eucalcemic, and hypercalcemic.

RESULTS: There were 1270 participants enrolled in our primary study, of whom 1047 arrived by EMS from the scene meeting inclusion for this analysis. Of these, 235 were hypocalcemic and 39 were hypercalcemic upon arrival. Patients with calcium derangements had lower survival compared to patients without derangements. Of those who were hypocalcemic, 32.8% received prehospital blood products, compared to 25.6% of those who were hypercalcemic upon arrival. There were 5 (12.8%) who were hypercalcemic that received prehospital calcium, potentially indicating iatrogenic hypercalcemia. Elevated prehospital shock indices were associated with both derangements. Of the 718 who received no fluids or blood, 116 (16.1%) were hypocalcemic and 27 (3.7%) were hypocalcemic with 2 hypercalcemic participants receiving calcium. Of those 136 that received a blood product prehospital, 77 were hypocalcemic (56.6%) with 1 receiving calcium, and 10 (7.4%) were hypercalcemic with 3 receiving calcium, and the remaining were eucalcemic with 4 (2.9%) receiving calcium.

CONCLUSIONS: Both hypocalcemia and hypercalcemia occurred in the setting of blood product and no blood product administration. Our study suggests that currently available assessment methods are inadequate for predicting the presence of a calcium derangement, both high and low.

CLINICALTRIALS: gov registration: NCT05885256.

Full text via DOI

item.title: The blunt truth: The role of marijuana in PTSD after intentional traumatic injury.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Kern JA, Wilson C, Joshi SA et al.

BACKGROUND: Survivors of interpersonal violence experience high rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and rates of marijuana use are rising among young adults. There is however, limited understanding of marijuana use patterns among survivors of interpersonal violence with PTSD. We evaluated relationships between PTSD and marijuana use following injury and hypothesized that PTSD-positive patients would report elevated follow-up marijuana use.

METHODS: Between 10/2019 and 7/1/2024, we prospectively collected data on patient demographics, PTSD, substance use (including marijuana), and PROMIS-29 quality of life domains for adult trauma patients admitted to an urban, academic, level-1 trauma center. Participants were screened at baseline and at 6- or 12-month follow-up. Injury characteristics were collected from the institutional trauma registry. Among the intentionally injured, we compared patients by follow-up PTSD screening results. We excluded patients who screened positive for PTSD at baseline. Using multivariable logistic regression we assessed relationships between follow-up PTSD and marijuana use, including demographic and injury characteristics as covariates. Our primary outcome was dichotomized follow-up marijuana use.

RESULTS: Of 105 participants injured by intentional trauma with complete follow-up data, 69 screened negative for PTSD at baseline and therefore were included in this analysis. Patients who screened positive for PTSD at follow-up had greater marijuana use at baseline (29% vs 3%, p = 0.002) and follow-up (42% vs 13%, p = 0.007), and worse PROMIS-29 scores in all domains (p ≤ 0.01), compared to PTSD-negative patients. In multivariable analysis, screening positive for PTSD was associated with 7.1 times greater odds of marijuana use at follow-up (p = 0.007, CI:1.7, 29.5).

CONCLUSIONS: PTSD and marijuana use were closely associated in survivors of interpersonal violence. Screening efforts should account for marijuana use specifically. Routine screening for marijuana use could improve recognition of psychological challenges after trauma and could help identify patients at risk for development of PTSD.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

item.title: Peripheral nerve blocks reduce opioid requirements in the first 24 h following surgical fixation of acute tibial shaft fractures.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic, Systems/QI] [weak match]
Khan UA, Quigley C, Schulman M et al.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of peripheral nerve blocks (PNB) on postoperative opioid use, length of stay (LOS), and incidence of acute compartment syndrome (ACS) in patients presenting with acute tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nail (IMN) fixation.

METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study Setting: Level 1 Academic Trauma Center from 2018 to 2022. Patient Selection Criteria: Patients aged 18-79 years with acute AO/OTA 42A-C tibial shaft fractures treated with IMN within 7 days of injury Outcome Measures and Comparisons: The primary outcome was postoperative opioid use, measured in morphine milligram equivalents (MME), during hospital stay, up to a maximum of 72 h after surgery. Patients who received a preoperative PNB were compared to those who did not receive a block. Secondary outcomes included postoperative LOS and incidence of ACS.

RESULTS: 246 patients were eligible for analysis of which 78 (32%) received a PNB (PNB=yes) and 168 (68%) did not (PNB=no). Mean MME were significantly lower in the PNB=yes group compared to the PNB=no group at 24 h (73 vs. 138, p < 0.001). Controlling for age, Injury Severity Score (ISS), and time to surgery, a multivariable regression model demonstrated a 36% reduction in MME per hour for patients that received PNBs. There were 3 cases of ACS in PNB=No and 1 in PNB=Yes. All 3 patients without a PNB were diagnosed within 2 days of surgery and underwent uncomplicated fasciotomies. One patient with a PNB re-presented to the hospital 5 days postoperatively, underwent fasciotomies, and was found to have anterior and lateral compartment necrosis.

CONCLUSION: PNBs for select acute tibial shaft fractures treated with IMN were associated with decreased opioid requirements in the first 24 h after surgery. No effect was noted beyond 24 h after surgery. Extreme vigilance is essential in patients with tibia fractures to monitor for ACS, especially when PNB is utilized.

item.title: The downside of the pull-up: A 10-year national analysis of emergency department visits, 2015-2024.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, TBI] [weak match]
Shabbir R, Layton B, Kang Z et al.

BACKGROUND: To characterize the epidemiology and clinical patterns of injuries related to pull-up and chin-up bars in a nationally representative emergency department (ED) dataset.

METHODS: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission National Electronic Injury Surveillance System from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2024. Cases were identified using product code 3277 with narrative filters for "pull-up," "chin-up," and "doorway bar," excluding barbells and playground equipment. NEISS sampling weights produced national estimates. Annual totals with 95 % confidence intervals were calculated and reported. Injury characteristics were summarized by age group, body region, diagnosis, location, disposition, and a narrative-derived mechanism category (fall, struck by bar, slip or detachment, other).

RESULTS: An estimated 40,987 ED visits were attributed to pull-up bar injuries, averaging about 4000 per year, with a peak in 2024 (5421; 95 % CI, 5315-5527). Patients were predominantly male (66.1 %) with a bimodal age distribution centered on children 5-14 years and adults 18-34 years. Craniofacial trauma predominated, with head and face together comprising nearly one-half of presentations, followed by upper-extremity involvement, including shoulder, wrist, and forearm. Laceration, internal head injury, and fracture were the leading diagnoses, with sprain or strain and contusion also frequent. Most incidents occurred in the home, and 93.8 % of patients were treated and released. Falls were the most common mechanism, followed by struck-by events and a subset explicitly involving bar slip or detachment.

CONCLUSIONS: Pull-up bar injuries constitute a consistent national burden of craniofacial and upper-extremity trauma concentrated in youth and young adults, largely managed nonoperatively in acute care settings. Improved recognition of exercise-associated injury mechanisms may assist diagnostic accuracy and reduce the burden on emergency and orthopedic services.

item.title: How the cause of surgical delay affects mortality in fragility hip fractures: A cohort study.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Senan R, Karthik P, Dhilon P et al.

BACKGROUND: Prompt surgery for fragility hip fractures is a cornerstone of care and a key metric within the Best Practice Tariff (BPT) in the United Kingdom. Yet, since 2011, time to theatre has steadily increased, BPT adherence has fallen, and paradoxically, mortality has reduced. It is still unclear if surgical delay is an independent predictor of mortality. Emerging evidence suggests that the causes of surgical delays may be more important determinants of mortality than the delay itself.

METHODS: A cohort study of 1769 hip fracture patients above the age of 60 was conducted in a single centre in England. This study collected demographic data, timing to theatre (<36 h vs ≥36 h), reasons for any delays, 30-day mortality and 1-year mortality between March 2020 and December 2024.

RESULTS: The most common cause of delay was insufficient theatre capacity (N = 365, 20.6%), followed by delays awaiting medical stabilisation (N = 102, 5.8%). Age (Χ

CONCLUSIONS: While early surgery remains beneficial, patients delayed solely due to administrative reasons did not demonstrate an associated increase in mortality. Mortality associated with operative delay was primarily associated amongst patients with concurrent acute illnesses and co-morbidities, independently increasing risk. To improve mortality, the focus must remain on pre-operative optimisation and robust orthogeriatric assessment, rather than surgical timing alone. Future iterations of the BPT may benefit from incorporating the cause of delay and physiological risk stratification to surgical timing targets to better align national incentives with clinical outcomes.

item.title: An anti-inflammatory melanocortin fusion polypeptide augments whole blood resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock in a rodent polytrauma model.
item.description:
J Trauma Acute Care Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Haemorrhage] [strong match]
Kim JH, Neidig LE, Ringgold KM et al.

BACKGROUND: Severe trauma induces a cytokine storm that is associated with impaired resuscitation and recovery. We investigated the impact of AQB-565, an anti-inflammatory melanocortin fusion polypeptide, as a novel treatment adjunct for whole blood resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock using a rat polytrauma shock model.

METHODS: Hemorrhagic shock with polytrauma was induced in 64 Sprague-Dawley rats. The rats were randomized to receive one of four intravenous treatments at 15 minutes posthemorrhage (T15): saline control, AQB-565, tranexamic acid (TXA), or combined AQB-565+ TXA. The rats were given autologous transfusion of shed whole blood at 60 minutes and as needed thereafter to achieve mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 60 mm Hg for up to 3 hours. Survival, hemodynamics, cytokine profiles, and hemorrhage volumes were compared between groups.

RESULTS: There was a significant overall effect of treatment group on MAP (two-way rmANOVA p=0.02) that coincided with blood transfusion. MAP was significantly increased at T105 with AQB-565+TXA versus saline control (p=0.046). Inflammatory plasma cytokines, including interleukin-6, were significantly decreased with AQB-565 versus control groups (ANOVA p values ≤0.01). Seventeen (26.6%) rats died before 3 hours. There was a trend towards increased survival for treatments containing AQB-565 versus controls that was not statistically significant (Kaplan-Meier log rank p=0.06).

CONCLUSIONS: A melanocortin pathway-activating polypeptide suppressed inflammation and improved hemodynamic response to whole blood transfusion in this hemorrhagic shock model.

Full text via DOI

item.title: Addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures reduces interfragmentary displacement - a biomechanical human cadaveric study.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [weak match]
Deichsel A, Große-Allermann A, Horst K et al.

PURPOSE: To investigate whether the addition of a McLaughlin cerclage to locking plate fixation of distal patellar pole fractures provides improved biomechanical construct stability and reduced interfragmentary displacement.

METHODS: A distal patellar pole fracture was simulated in sixteen fresh-frozen human cadaveric knees by a horizontal osteotomy in the distal third of the patella. Subsequently, locking plate fixation was performed. In a randomized half of the specimens, an additional McLaughlin wire cerclage was applied. The specimens were then subjected to 3000 cycles of extension starting at 90° of flexion under a maximum tensile load of 320 N. Using a Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system, the interfragmentary displacement between the proximal and distal fragments was measured at 1, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 3000 cycles. Statistical analysis was performed using repeated-measures ANOVA and Welch's unpaired t-t test at 3000 cycles.

RESULTS: An additional McLaughlin cerclage significantly reduced interfragmentary displacement under cyclic loading in comparison to locking plate fixation alone. After 3000 cycles, displacement was 2.27 ± 1.84 mm with plate fixation alone and 0.36 ± 0.22 mm with additional McLaughlin cerclage (mean difference 1.91 mm; 95% CI 0.38-3.45 mm; p = 0.0215).

CONCLUSION: An additional McLaughlin cerclage reduced interfragmentary displacement in distal patellar pole fractures. In cases of unstable distal pole patella fractures, the additional use of a McLaughlin cerclage may therefore be considered to enhance construct stability.

item.title: Trauma care performance and patient outcomes - insights from a major trauma centre in Sweden.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma, Penetrating, Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Eriksson J, Larsson E, Arnason B et al.

PURPOSE: Trauma is a leading cause of death among individuals under 45 years of age. Evaluating trauma system performance over time is important but inherently difficult due to concurrent changes in patient demographics, case-mix and care processes. The aim of this study was to describe temporal changes in patient demographics, injury severity and trauma care at a major trauma centre in Sweden from 2017 to 2023. We hypothesised that risk-adjusted 30-day mortality decreased and that time to computed tomography was reduced over the study period.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the Karolinska Trauma Registry, including all trauma patients aged > 15 years fulfilling criteria for full trauma team activation, admitted between January 2017 and August 2023. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess changes in 30-day mortality over time, adjusted for age, sex, injury severity category, ASA score and injury type. Time from arrival to computed tomography was analysed by linear regression and, because the distribution was skewed, by quantile (median) regression.

RESULTS: A total of 5,615 trauma patients were included. Over the study period, the patient population became older, and ASA scores increased, while injury severity and the proportion of penetrating injury remained unchanged. In multivariable logistic regression with 2017 as reference, the odds of 30-day mortality in 2022-2023 were lower (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.88, P = 0.008) after adjusting for confounders. Median time to computed tomography decreased from 31 to 21 min; the adjusted difference in 2022-2023 compared with 2017 was - 7.5 min by linear regression (P = 0.014) and - 10.4 min by quantile regression (95% CI - 11.5 to - 9.2, P < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Our findings are consistent with improvements in trauma care within a mature trauma system, with shorter median time to computed tomography and lower 30-day mortality despite an aging population with increasing comorbidity. However, the specific drivers of these changes are difficult to identify, and future studies should explore how individual components of pre-hospital and in-hospital care contribute to trauma outcomes.

item.description:

item.title: Peripheral vascular trauma in a civilian Asian trauma centre: Epidemiology, management and outcomes over 9 years.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Penetrating, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Chong FJ, Lee KRY, Go K et al.

BACKGROUND: Peripheral vascular injuries (PVI) are uncommon but potentially limb-threatening complications of extremity trauma. Most existing literature originates from military settings or Western trauma systems. We aimed to describe the epidemiology, management strategies, and outcomes of traumatic PVI in a civilian tertiary trauma centre in Singapore.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the institutional trauma registry of Tan Tock Seng Hospital between January 2013 and December 2021. Patients presenting with upper or lower extremity vascular injuries were identified using Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) coding. Demographics, injury characteristics, anatomical injury patterns, interventions, and outcomes including limb salvage, complications, and inpatient mortality were analysed. Comparisons between upper and lower limb injuries were performed using appropriate statistical tests.

RESULTS: Among 77,990 trauma admissions, 180 patients sustained PVI (incidence 0.23%). Median age was 36 years and 87% were male. Overall, penetrating trauma was more common (58.9%), but lower limb injuries were predominantly due to blunt trauma (68%), particularly road traffic accidents. Lower limb PVIs were associated with higher injury severity than upper limb PVIs (p < 0.001). Operative management was required in most arterial and venous injuries. Primary repair and endovascular interventions demonstrated excellent limb salvage, whereas bypass procedures were associated with lower salvage rates. Overall limb salvage for lower limb PVI was 88%, with an amputation rate of 10% and mortality of 3%. Most (93%) were functionally independent at discharge.

CONCLUSIONS: PVI predominantly affects young male patients and are commonly associated with blunt trauma from road traffic accidents. Despite significant injury severity, favourable limb salvage and functional outcomes can be achieved with timely multidisciplinary management. These findings highlight the importance of coordinated multidisciplinary trauma care in optimizing outcomes following extremity vascular trauma.

item.title: New developments in locking plate osteosynthesis - A narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Braun BJ, Roßlenbroich S, Menger MM et al.

Plate osteosynthesis has evolved significantly, progressing from the first plates with externally protruding screws to anatomically precontoured systems designed for minimally invasive application. In this narrative review, we provide a brief recap of the history of locked plating and highlight the most relevant developments of the last two decades. These include anatomical innovations and mechanobiologically optimized plates, as well as emerging systems capable of monitoring the fracture healing progress.

item.title: The use of PMMA bone cement in trauma surgery: A narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [strong match]
Holla M, Migdad H, Blokhuis T

BACKGROUND: Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement has been used for decades in orthopaedic surgery, primarily for fixation of endoprostheses. In trauma surgery, its role is more heterogeneous and often underappreciated.

METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the material properties, biological behavior, and clinical applications of PMMA in trauma surgery, including prosthesis fixation, screw augmentation, and its use as a temporary spacer. Finally, the use of PMMA used as a permanent spacer, including technical tips is described.

RESULTS: PMMA provides high compressive strength, minimal shrinkage, and reliable handling characteristics. Cement augmentation improves implant anchorage in osteoporotic bone. As a spacer, PMMA plays a key role in staged reconstruction. Finally, in selected patients and as a salvage procedure, PMMA may function as a permanent load-sharing implant when combined with stable internal fixation.

CONCLUSION: PMMA remains a versatile, inexpensive, and widely available tool in trauma surgery beyond its classical role in arthroplasty.

item.title: Surface topography and nanostructural modifications for the prevention of bacterial infections.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Graziani G, Ghezzi D

Implant-associated infections represent severe complications in orthopaedics and trauma surgery, largely driven by early bacterial adhesion and subsequent biofilm formation on device surfaces. The increasing incidence of multidrug-resistant pathogens further complicates management and underscores the urgent need for preventive, antibiotic-free strategies. Surface functionalization of implantable metals has emerged as a key approach to inhibit bacterial colonization at the implant-tissue interface while minimizing systemic toxicity and selective pressure for resistance. This review provides a comprehensive and clinically oriented overview of two major surface-based strategies: micro/nano-scale surface patterning (non-releasing approaches) and nanostructured antibacterial metallic coatings (releasing or contact-killing systems). Surface patterning modifies topography, wettability, and surface charge to reduce bacterial adhesion or induce mechanical disruption of bacterial membranes. Although highly promising in vitro and not reliant on the release of antimicrobial agents, hence not inserting compounds with potential toxicity, current evidence indicates that patterned surfaces alone often provide limited and transient protection in vivo, where protein adsorption and complex microbial communities may mask topographical effects. In contrast, nanostructured antibacterial metallic coatings offer broad-spectrum antibacterial and antibiofilm activity through ion release and/or contact-mediated mechanisms. Advances in plasma-assisted deposition technologies, including magnetron sputtering, pulsed laser deposition, and ionized jet deposition, enable precise control over coating thickness, morphology, and ion-release kinetics, thereby enhancing antibacterial efficacy while preserving biocompatibility and osteogenic potential. Recent in vivo data support the durability and safety of thin nanostructured coatings, highlighting their translational potential. Although not-yet clinically available, due to challenges in clinical translation of biomedical devices, these strategies can build a new generation of antibacterial device, with efficacy targeted to the microbial community and to tackling biofilm. Comparative observations suggest that while surface patterning represents a valuable complementary strategy, nanostructured metallic thin films currently provide more robust and clinically relevant antimicrobial performance. Future research should prioritize standardized antibiofilm testing models, validation in complex in vivo settings, combination strategies integrating patterning and coatings, and the rational tuning of multi-metal systems to address heterogeneous microbial communities.

item.title: Cerclage wiring: Innovations and applications.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Förch S, Sandriesser S, Fenwick A et al.

Immediate full weight-bearing of osteosynthesis constructs is gaining increasing importance in modern trauma surgery. Many geriatric patients cannot reliably adhere to partial weight-bearing instructions, and younger patients may benefit from accelerated rehabilitation enabled by early full weight-bearing. In this context, an older technique of minimally invasive cerclage fixation of the tibia is receiving renewed attention. The surgical technique has been adapted to contemporary cerclage systems and biomechanically evaluated for the first time. Several studies using synthetic and cadaveric bone models have demonstrated that modern cable cerclages, particularly in spiral fractures, are capable of significantly increasing the stiffness of both locking plate and intramedullary nail osteosyntheses, provided that anatomical reduction is achieved through the cerclage. From a biomechanical standpoint, the additive cerclage thus enables immediate postoperative full weight-bearing. Early clinical studies suggest, that minimally invasive tibial cerclage can be applied without an increased complication rate and is associated with faster rehabilitation and higher patient satisfaction in the early postoperative phase. Although evidence is limited, the principle of additive cerclage appears to be transferable to humeral shaft spiral fractures.

item.title: Overview and new developments in intramedullary and cephalomedullary nailing.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Hackl S, Weisemann F, Trapp O et al.

The primary objectives of osteosynthetic fracture stabilization are accurate fracture reduction, restoration of the anatomical axis and rotational alignment, and the provision of adequate biomechanical and biological conditions to support bone healing. In fractures of long tubular bones, these goals can be optimally achieved by intramedullary nailing, which provides long-segment internal splinting along the anatomical axis of the bone combined with locking screws to ensure axial and rotational stability. In addition, intramedullary nailing is a tissue-preserving technique, as nail insertion is performed remote from the fracture site, thereby minimizing soft tissue trauma within the fracture zone. The indications for intramedullary nailing include epiphyseal and diaphyseal fractures of long bones, selected metaphyseal fractures that can be stabilized using anatomically contoured nails, as well as reconstructive procedures such as the treatment of nonunions, corrective osteotomies, and arthrodeses of the lower extremity. A major advantage of intramedullary nailing is the high primary stability of the implant, which generally allows early functional rehabilitation. The resulting biomechanical benefits permit early full weight bearing and, in the treatment of fracture healing disorders, are associated with high rates of osseous union. Continuous improvements in implant design and instrumentation, together with the introduction of anatomically contoured reconstruction nails, are expected to further expand the indications and effectiveness of intramedullary nailing. This narrative review summarizes historical milestones, biomechanical principles, technical aspects, and recent implant developments in intramedullary nailing, with a particular focus on cephalomedullary nailing for unstable trochanteric and subtrochanteric femoral fractures. Special emphasis is placed on fracture reduction quality, implant selection, and screw positioning, as these factors remain the strongest determinants of fixation stability and clinical outcome.

item.title: Review of a "Bone Glue Fixation" development.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Procter P

The paper presents some of the background to the development of bone glues. Whilst there have been many attempts over the last 100 years to find a safe and effective biomimetic adhesive biomaterial it is only recently that promising and feasible candidates have been developed. In particular a formulation based on a combination of an amino acid, phosphoserine (PSer), together with calcium salts and water, has demonstrated the potential to meet clinically defined requirements for a bone adhesive (Osstic®). This bone glue has achieved first in human use after having demonstrated consistent preclinical performance.

item.title: Alternate non-metallic implants in fracture care - A review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Fritz T, Osche D, Liodakis E et al.

The use of implants in the treatment of fractures evolved over the last decades. Until today, most implant designs are based on metallic alloys such as Titanium or stainless steel. However, the global ageing population with increasing numbers of fragility and pathological fractures challenges current implant designs regarding stress shielding, fragile soft tissue and advanced demands like reduced imaging artefacts for radiotherapy planning. Therefore, alternative non-metallic implants that more closely resemble the mechanical properties of bone or provide additional stability as intramedullary augmentation have become available. This narrative-review summarizes the current available (2026) technology, biomechanical properties, clinical applications, outcomes and complications of CFR-PEEK implants and photodynamic bone stabilization implants in fracture management. In total n = 100 publications were taken into consideration for this narrative-review. Non-metallic-implants for fracture care are still a niche product in the treatment of fractures. However, with the ageing population and the increasing number of impaired bone quality and stability, these methods could help reduce stress shielding and force distribution comparable to physiological bone (CFR-PEEK implants) or allow additional augmentation (photodynamic bone stabilization) in reduced bone quality.

item.title: Innovation in external fixation: Emerging hardware, software and automation technologies.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic] [weak match]
Raj S, Fornasiero M, Tsang SJ

External fixation remains a cornerstone of contemporary orthopaedic trauma and limb reconstruction surgery. While the biological principles for bone healing and regeneration established by Ilizarov continue to underpin modern practice, significant technological innovation has occurred over the past two decades. These developments have focused on improving construct stability, enhancing deformity correction accuracy, reducing technical complexity and improving the patient experience. Advances in hardware design have expanded fixation options and increased the adaptability of circular frames in complex trauma and reconstructive settings. Parallel developments in software have transformed deformity analysis, preoperative planning and correction execution through improved registration systems, virtual frame construction and cloud-based treatment platforms. More recently, remote patient support systems and automated strut technologies have sought to reduce the treatment burden associated with prolonged frame use. This review examines contemporary innovations in external fixation, focusing on developments in hardware, software, patient engagement technologies and automation. The available evidence is critically appraised and future directions explored. While many innovations demonstrate clear theoretical and practical advantages, robust clinical evidence remains limited for several emerging technologies. Nevertheless, the convergence of advanced engineering, digital health technologies and artificial intelligence is likely to fundamentally reshape the future of external fixation.

item.title: Modernizing preoperative planning in orthopaedic trauma surgery.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic] [strong match]
Leland CR, Farid AR, Stenquist DS et al.

Preoperative planning in orthopaedic trauma remains largely experience-driven despite advances in imaging and predictive modeling. Although three-dimensional (3D) reconstructions improve fracture visualization, they do not routinely predict biomechanical stability across competing fixation strategies. Automated segmentation and finite element analysis (FEA) offer the potential to transition trauma planning from primarily anatomic to a method by which constructs may be optimized. This narrative review summarizes the current state of 3D planning and segmentation, describes the principles and established applications of FEA, delineates the workflow of finite element modeling in clinical practice, and integrates representative clinical cases to illustrate how plate positioning and screw configuration affect construct stability and works alongside the surgeon to help inform decisions. Broader implications for hospital systems, patients, and industry are discussed, along with future integration into navigation, robotics, and intraoperative 3D imaging workflows.

item.title: Patient-specific instrument with 3D printing technology in orthopaedic trauma: A narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic] [strong match]
Wong PY, Liu C, Tao H et al.

3D printing technology has been increasingly used in orthopaedic surgery. Current literature has demonstrated the benefits of applying 3D printing in orthopaedic trauma with the use of patient-specific instruments (PSI) including surgical guides and implants on selected bone fracture regions. This narrative review outlines the development of PSI including the navigation templates and implants using 3D printing technology. A comprehensive summary was presented for the application and effectiveness of PSI for fracture treatment in the upper extremities, pelvic region and lower extremities surgeries, particularly in regards to operative time, surgical accuracy and functional outcomes. 3D-printed patient-specific navigation guide had been used in reduction and fixation surgeries such as for navigating Kirschner wires (K-wire) insertion and screw placement in different bone fracture regions. PSI significantly increased surgical accuracy of K-wire insertion and screw placements, with significant reduction in operative time. For functional outcomes, 3D-printed navigation guide was comparable to conventional surgery. There are increasing studies exploring the clinical feasibility of patient-specific metal implant using 3D printing technology with advantage of high accuracy in fracture surgeries. Future studies to investigate the clinical efficacy of the patient-specific metal implants are warranted.

item.title: Generation Z and engagement in orthopaedic trauma: A multigenerational qualitative study.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic] [strong match]
Blokhuis TJ, Holla M, Gomez Vallejo J et al.

BACKGROUND: Healthcare systems face increasing demand due to population ageing and workforce shortages. At the same time, Generation Z is entering surgical training. Their work values may differ from those of previous generations, potentially affecting engagement in demanding specialties such as orthopaedic trauma surgery. This study explores multigenerational perspectives on professional identity, work intensity, academic engagement, and work-life integration within orthopaedic trauma.

METHODS: Prior to the 2024 Leadership Forum of the Osteosynthesis and Trauma Care Foundation (OTCF), a standardized questionnaire consisting of declarative statements rated on a five-point Likert scale was distributed to orthopaedic trauma residents and senior consultants from international chapters. During the Forum, a moderated multigenerational discussion was conducted. The session was recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic qualitative analysis.

RESULTS: Eight residents and fifteen consultants from Europe, North America, South America, Africa, and Asia participated. Across generations, intensive training was considered essential for achieving surgical mastery. However, younger participants emphasized work-life boundaries, institutional recognition of non-clinical work, and psychological safety. Senior surgeons more frequently described their profession as central to their identity and viewed unpaid academic engagement as intrinsic to surgical responsibility.

CONCLUSION: Generation Z trainees demonstrate strong commitment to orthopaedic trauma but differ from senior surgeons in expectations regarding professional identity, uncompensated academic work, and work-life integration. Recognition of evolving professional values is critical for workforce sustainability and intergenerational collaboration in trauma surgery.

item.title: Tight rope fixation in fracture management.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Keating JF

The use of tightrope fixation using metal buttons linked by suture material was first reported in 2005 when their use was suggested as an alternative to syndesmosis screws in ankle fractures associated with a diastasis. These implants are now used widely as a component of fixation in ankle fractures with a diastasis. The published results of their use in these injuries have shown that they are an effective method of treating diastasis of the ankle tibio-fibular syndesmosis with some evidence to suggest that they have a lower rate of malunion, fewer implant related complications, a reduced need for implant removal and in some trials better functional outcomes than screw fixation. Variations of these devices have also been used for fixation of lateral third clavicular fractures and acromioclavicular dislocations. Their use alone or in combination with plate fixation has been shown to be an effective method of fixation of lateral third clavicle fractures with a low rate of malunion and implant related problems. They have also shown to be an effective method of treatment for acromioclavicular dislocation, although there is still debate about the role of surgical treatment for these injuries. There are miscellaneous reports of their use for other fractures and dislocations in other anatomic locations notably for Lisfranc injuries in the foot. Better quality prospective clinical studies are still needed to define their exact role in fracture management.

item.title: Adherent antimicrobial coatings for orthopaedic implants - A narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma] [weak match]
Montali A, D'Este M, Moriarty TF et al.

There is a broad consensus among orthopaedic and trauma surgeons, as well as infection specialists, that antibacterial coatings represent an important tool for both the prevention and management of fracture-related infections. Nonetheless, the choice of commercially available implants fitted with an antibacterial coating remains limited. Intramedullary nails with resorbable, antibiotic eluting coatings have been commercially available for over a decade. Although multiple case series have shown evidence of efficacy of antimicrobial orthopaedic implants, randomized controlled trials are still lacking and their uptake in everyday clinical practice has been slow. More recently, nails with galvanic noble metal coatings were introduced, with encouraging clinical results. The most widely used coatings with the longest clinical track record are silver coated joint replacement endoprostheses, which have been successfully employed in revision surgeries and in patients undergoing tumor-related procedures. Silver coated plates are on the verge of market introduction and will represent the first of their kind to be broadly available. Overall, adherent antibacterial coatings are showing beneficial outcomes in terms of safety and efficacy. Health-technology assessments show cost effectiveness, demonstrating that in higher risk patient populations, the additional cost of using a coated implant is significantly less than the cost of treating an infection. Regulatory hurdles remain high, especially in the USA, where, to be best of our knowledge, coated implants have not been approved yet. Driven by the clear clinical need, we anticipate a dynamic near future in this field, with progress moving toward establishing coated implants as the standard of care for appropriate patient populations and expanding the range of available coating solutions. Such developments will ultimately benefit patients, surgeons, and the overall healthcare system.

item.title: Distal femur plate-nail constructs. Belt and suspenders?
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [General Trauma, Orthopaedic] [weak match]
Chana-Rodríguez F, Rojo-Manaute JM, Latif GS et al.

Given the inherent complexity of distal femoral fractures and non-unions, management should be directed by an experienced orthopaedic trauma surgeon to ensure optimal reduction and stable fixation. This report describes the surgical technique of three cases managed with dual nail-plate fixation, supplemented by a review of contemporary literature regarding this hybrid construct. Evidence from meta-analyses suggests that combined fixation significantly minimizes total complications and reoperations compared to single-construct fixation in distal femur fractures. Notably, these clinical benefits are achieved without a significant increase in operative duration, blood loss, or hospital stay. However, the current literature is restricted to retrospective studies, underscoring the imperative for prospective randomized controlled trials to validate these clinical benefits.

item.title: Past, present and future of distal radius corrective osteotomy: From 2D based reconstruction to 3D data-driven, patient specific care.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Loonen TGJ, Maal TJJ, Edwards MJR et al.

Corrective osteotomy for distal radius malunion has evolved from two-dimensional (2D) radiograph based planning and surgeon performed geometric analysis to advanced three-dimensional (3D) virtual surgical planning (VSP). Historically guided by predefined radiographic parameters, contemporary practice increasingly emphasizes symptom severity and patient-specific functional goals. CT-based 3D models, contralateral surface matching, and patient-specific guides and implants have improved the accuracy of deformity correction. However, greater anatomical precision does not automatically translate into superior functional outcomes. Future progress depends on standardized evaluation frameworks, multicenter data collection, and predictive models to determine the clinical value of virtual surgical planning (VSP) and patient-specific implants (PSI) in delivering individualized, cost-effective and function-oriented care across the entire treatment pathway.

item.title: 3D printed scaffolds for reconstruction of segmental long bone defects: A mini narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Gilissen MJV, Lodewijks AJL, Vissers-Van der Broeck LCA et al.

Large segmental bone defects remain a major challenge in orthopedic reconstruction because successful healing requires both mechanical stability and coordinated biological regeneration. Although autologous bone grafting remains the clinical gold standard due to its osteogenic, osteoinductive, and osteoconductive properties, its application is limited by donor site morbidity, restricted graft availability, and increased operative burden. These limitations have stimulated the development of scaffold-based regenerative strategies aimed at restoring structural integrity while promoting bone regeneration. Recent advances in additive manufacturing have enabled the fabrication of patient-specific three-dimensional (3D) scaffolds with controlled architecture, porosity, and mechanical properties that approximate native bone structure. This mini-review summarizes recent developments in 3D-printed scaffolds for the reconstruction of long bone defects, with particular emphasis on differences between non-biodegradable metallic constructs and biodegradable polymeric, ceramic, and composite materials. Porous titanium scaffolds demonstrate high mechanical stability and early osteointegration, making them promising for extensive load-bearing defects, although concerns remain regarding long-term stress shielding and permanent implant retention. Biodegradable ceramics and polymer-based scaffolds offer improved biological integration and controlled degradation, but often require further optimization of mechanical stability and biological augmentation. Composite constructs combining polymers, ceramics, or bioactive metals aim to integrate structural support with enhanced osteogenic and angiogenic responses. Despite encouraging preclinical results and emerging early clinical applications, current evidence remains limited by small patient cohorts, heterogeneous scaffold designs, and insufficient long-term outcome data. Future studies should focus on standardized scaffold designs, comparative clinical trials, and long-term evaluation to clarify the optimal role of 3D-printed biomaterials in the treatment of large segmental bone defects.

item.title: Mini-fragment applications for lower extremity long bone fractures: A narrative review.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Dunbar RP, Sorkin AT, Alismaily HM et al.

Mini-fragment systems (2.0, 2.4 and 2.7 mm) have evolved from fixation of just hand and foot fractures to have become an indispensable component of complex fracture fixation all over the appendicular skeleton. Surgeons currently use mini-fragment fixation in provisional fixation capacities, as adjunctive fixation to larger fixation constructs and in isolation in select situations. The versatility and popularity of these implants is far reaching, even in the lower extremity long bones, where their usage may be somewhat non-intuitive. In this narrative review we delineate the rationale for the use of these implants. We then illustrate several applications for these implants throughout the lower extremities that have proven useful.

item.title: Izalontamab brengitecan for HR+/HER2- breast cancer in China (PANKU-Breast01): a randomised, phase 3 trial.
item.description:
Lancet | Tier 2 Filtered [Haemorrhage] [weak match]
Lan B, Shi Y, Shao X et al.

BACKGROUND: Patients with heavily pretreated hormone receptor-positive and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HR+/HER2-) breast cancer have few treatment options. Izalontamab brengitecan (iza-bren) is a first-in-class, epidermal growth factor receptor and HER3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate that contains a potent topoisomerase I inhibitor payload (Ed-04). The aim of PANKU-Breast01 was to compare the efficacy and safety of iza-bren versus chemotherapy in patients with pretreated HR+/HER2- breast cancer.

METHODS: In this randomised, phase 3, open-label, multicentre study in 72 hospitals in China, patients with HR+/HER2- breast cancer who had disease progression after endocrine therapy, cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) 4/6 inhibitors, and one or two lines of chemotherapy were randomly assigned (1:1) to iza-bren (2·5 mg/kg, administered by intravenous infusion on day 1 and day 8 every 3 weeks) or physician's choice chemotherapy (eribulin, 1·4 mg/m

FINDINGS: Between April 24, 2024, and June 6, 2025, 560 patients were screened, 177 were excluded, and 383 patients were randomly assigned and treated (190 were assigned to the iza-bren group and 193 were assigned to the chemotherapy group). All 383 participants in the study were female and of Chinese ethnicity. Median age was 54·0 years (IQR 47·0-60·0). At data cutoff (July 21, 2026), median follow-up for progression-free survival was 15·2 months (95% CI 13·9-16·8). Iza-bren significantly improved progression-free survival versus chemotherapy (log-rank p<0·0001), and median progression-free survival assessed by Blinded Independent Central Review was 8·2 months (95% CI 6·9-8·6) versus 4·0 months (2·9-4·3; HR 0·41 [95% CI 0·33-0·53]). Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 162 (85%) patients in the iza-bren group versus 127 (66%) patients in the chemotherapy group, and haematological adverse events were the most common in both groups. For the treatment of haematological adverse events, 138 (73%) patients in the iza-bren group received platelet-elevating agents, 28 (15%) patients in the iza-bren group received platelet transfusion, and 18 patients (10%) in the iza-bren group received a blood transfusion. Two patients in the iza-bren group died due to treatment-related adverse events.

INTERPRETATION: Iza-bren showed a significant improvement in progression-free survival versus chemotherapy in patients with HR+/HER2- breast cancer previously treated with endocrine therapy, CDK4/6 inhibitors, and one or two lines of chemotherapy (including taxanes). The overall survival data were immature, and an overall survival benefit has not been established. These results suggest that iza-bren could be a new treatment option for this population in China; however, further evaluation of iza-bren in global populations and in earlier lines of therapy for HER2-negative breast cancer is warranted.

FUNDING: Baili-Bio (Chengdu) Pharmaceutical, CAMS Innovation Fund for Medical Sciences, Noncommunicable Chronic Diseases-National Science and Technology Major Project, National High Level Hospital Clinical Research Funding, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

item.title: Quantitative decision-support strategies to enhance emergency medical service accessibility in high-risk freeway tunnels.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [Prehospital] [weak match]
Jung S, Qin X

Crashes inside road tunnels often result in more severe outcomes due to spatial constraints that delay prehospital emergency medical services (EMS) access. Emergency evacuation facilities, such as cross passages and emergency parking areas, are critical for ensuring timely EMS response during traffic congestion caused by in-tunnel crashes. This study presents a quantitative approach to develop targeted strategies for enhancing such facilities to improve EMS accessibility in tunnels. Nationwide in-tunnel crash data from Korean freeways over a four-year period were analyzed, and the limited number of severe crash cases was addressed using SMOTE-based data augmentation to balance severity levels in the prediction model. A SHAP-based XGBoost classifier was applied to identify the influence of key features related to EMS accessibility and emergency evacuation facilities on crash severity. The results showed that crashes occurring more than 1 km from the tunnel entrance and EMS response coverage within a 10-15 km range have a significant impact on increasing crash severity. The presence of emergency cross passages, three or more lanes, emergency parking areas, and properly spaced CCTV installations were found to help reduce crash severity. Based on these findings, tunnels with particularly limited EMS accessibility were prioritized, and tailored facility improvement measures were proposed. This study provides quantitative evidence to guide cost-effective upgrades of tunnel emergency evacuation facilities, enhancing prehospital EMS accessibility and emergency preparedness. The proposed methodology can also support decision-making on implementing road tunnel safety improvement policies.

item.title: Single crash, multiple stories: A finite mixture perspective of motorcycle injury severity with a focus on post-crash medical, rescue, human and roadway-environmental factors.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [Prehospital, Systems/QI] [strong match]
Zia-Ur-Rehman, Ahmad N, Ahmed A et al.

This study investigates the factors, including post-crash medical conditions (i.e., Glasgow Coma Score "GCS", Systolic Blood Pressure "SBP"), emergency response (i.e., pre-hospital time and mode of evacuation), human factors, and roadway-environment, affecting the Injury Severity Score (ISS) in motorcycle crashes. Utilizing a comprehensive hospital-based dataset in Karachi, Pakistan, and after addressing the issues of missing or inappropriate values via synthetic data generation, a Tobit regression (baseline) model was first employed in a corner solution setup. Harnessing 204,503 hospital-based motorcycle crash records (2007-2015) from Karachi (Pakistan), missing and inappaorpirate values were addressed through synthetic data generation. A baseline model and a finite mixture Tobit model (accounting for unobserved heterogeneity) were employed. The findings from the baseline model indicate that compared to mild/normal GCS (13-15) and SBP (> 89 mmHg), for crash victims with severe GCS (3-8) and severely low SBP (2-49 mmHg), the ISS significantly increases by 4.5249 and 7.8042 units, respectively. A positive non-linear association between prehospital time (PHT) and ISS was established. The baseline model recognizes over-speeding, nighttime crashes, wrong-way riding or driving, and involvement of multiple vehicles to significantly increase ISS by 0.1909, 0.0198, 0.0787, and 0.3333 units, respectively. The finite mixture Tobit model identifies two latent classes of crash victims with dissimilar ISS patterns and varying relationships of key correlates with ISS, indicating that reliance on a standard Tobit model could lead to misleading inferences. The practical implications are discussed in the paper.

item.title: Chest tube fixation strength depends on suture caliber and fixation technique rather than tube diameter: a biomechanical cadaver study.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [General Trauma] [weak match]
Fricke JJ, Schöbel T, Meißner R et al.

BACKGROUND: Chest tube dislodgement remains a relevant complication in emergency, trauma, and intensive care medicine. In a previous biomechanical study, the Modified Johannesburg technique using Mersilene USP 1 demonstrated superior fixation strength compared with other chest tube fixation techniques. The present study aimed to determine whether suture size, suture material, and chest tube diameter influence fixation strength.

METHODS: A prospective interventional biomechanical cadaveric study was performed using fresh porcine thoracic wall specimens. A total of 320 load-to-failure tests were conducted under standardized laboratory conditions. Two fixation techniques, Modified Johannesburg and Purse String, were compared using two chest tube diameters (20/28 Ch) and four non-absorbable braided suture configurations: Mersilene USP 1, Mersilene USP 2 - 0, Silk USP 1, and Silk USP 2 - 0. Each experimental group consisted of 20 specimens. Specimens were tested in a uniaxial testing machine until construct failure. Force [N] and elongation [mm] at failure were measured. The experiments were videotaped, and the failure mechanism was analyzed.

RESULTS: The Modified Johannesburg technique demonstrated significantly higher pull-out forces compared to the Purse String technique (125.0 vs. 66.4 N; p < 0.001), as did larger suture sizes (USP 1 vs. 2 - 0; p < 0.001) and Mersilene compared to Silk (114.6 vs. 76.9 N; p < 0.001). Chest tube size had only a very small and inconsistent effect on pull-out strength. The predominant failure mode was suture rupture (94.7%).

CONCLUSIONS: Chest tube fixation strength is significantly influenced by fixation technique, suture size, and suture material. The effect of chest tube diameter on fixation strength appeared negligible. The Modified Johannesburg technique, size 1 sutures, and Mersilene material provided superior biomechanical stability. Since failure occurred predominantly by suture rupture, the suture appears to represent the weakest link of the fixation construct.

item.title: Changes in patellar height following suprapatellar and infrapatellar tibial nailing: a retrospective comparative cohort study.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [weak match]
Olivieri R, Hernández J, Soto JM et al.

PURPOSE: Patella baja has been described after infrapatellar tibial nailing and may contribute to postoperative knee morbidity; however, whether the nail insertion approach influences postoperative patellar height remains unclear. This study compared longitudinal changes in patellar height (PH) after suprapatellar and infrapatellar intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures. We hypothesized that the suprapatellar approach would better preserve patellar height.

METHODS: A retrospective comparative cohort study included 114 tibial shaft fractures treated with intramedullary nailing between 2016 and 2023, using a suprapatellar (n = 86) or infrapatellar (n = 28) approach. Patellar height was assessed using the Caton-Deschamps Index (CDI) on preoperative and final follow-up radiographs. The primary outcome was the longitudinal change in CDI (ΔCDI). Fracture union, complications, and reoperations were secondary outcomes.

RESULTS: The mean reduction in CDI was greater following infrapatellar than suprapatellar nailing (ΔCDI - 0.116 ± 0.173 vs. -0.011 ± 0.107; p = 0.001). After adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration, this association remained significant (adjusted β=-0.055; 95% CI - 0.107 to - 0.004; p = 0.035), although sensitivity analyses showed attenuation after additional adjustment for sex. Fracture union rates were similar between approaches (93.0% vs. 92.9%; p = 0.987), with no statistically significant differences in complications or reoperations.

CONCLUSION: Infrapatellar tibial nailing was associated with a significant postoperative reduction in PH compared with the suprapatellar approach. This association persisted after adjustment for baseline CDI and follow-up duration but was sensitive to additional adjustment for sex. These findings highlight a potential relationship between nail insertion approach and postoperative PH but do not establish an independent effect of surgical approach.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Retrospective cohort study (Level III).

item.title: Intraarticular calcaneal fractures: biomechanical analysis of two fixation constructs.
item.description:
Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg | Core Trauma [weak match]
Ziegenhain F, Zderic I, Zondervan R et al.

BACKGROUND: Whether endovascular therapy benefits patients with mild acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion involving the anterior circulation is uncertain.

The patients were randomly assigned to undergo endovascular therapy and receive medical management or to receive medical management alone. BACKGROUND: Endovascular thrombectomy is an established treatment for acute ischemic stroke. Whether the benefit extends to patients with salvageable brain tissue in the infarct who present more than 24 hours after symptom onset or the time when they were last known to be well is uncertain.

METHODS: We conducted an open-label, randomized trial with blinded outcome assessment at comprehensive stroke centers in China. Patients with acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and imaging-identified salvageable brain tissue at 24 to 72 hours were assigned to receive endovascular therapy plus standard medical care (intervention group) or standard medical care alone (control group). The primary outcome was functional status, defined by the score on the modified Rankin scale (range, 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater disability and a score of 6 indicating death) at 90 days, with results assessed as the distribution of scores in each group. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients who presented 24 to 72 hours after an acute ischemic stroke from large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation and had imaging-identified salvageable tissue, endovascular therapy resulted in better functional outcomes than standard care but led to a higher risk of intracranial hemorrhage and death. BACKGROUND: Severe trauma patients often need a large amount of blood transfusion including red blood cells (RBCs), fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelet. The blood transfusion can cause serious transfusion-related adverse events including respiratory complications, however, the risks of blood transfusion in trauma patients have not been well documented. The trial enrolled adult trauma patients transferred to the emergency department with severe bleeding or suspected severe bleeding and circulatory shock. All patients registered in this trial were included in this study. The primary outcome measure was the occurrence of respiratory failure within 7 days after admission. A logistic regression analysis on respiratory failure adjusted for sex, Injury Severity Score (ISS), chest Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) score, and the amount of RBCs, FFP, and platelet transfusions within 24 h was performed.

RESULTS: Of 417 trauma patients, 40 (9.8%) developed respiratory failure. Logistic regression analysis revealed that sex, chest AIS score, and platelet transfusion volume were associated with respiratory failure with 7 days after admission after adjustment (odds ratio [OR]: 0.300, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.113-0.794, p = 0.015, OR: 1.732, 95% CI: 1.267-2.367, p < 0.001, OR: 1.071, 95% CI: 1.021-1.122, p = 0.005 respectively). ISS, RBC, and FFP transfusions were not associated with respiratory failure (all p ≥ 0.05).

CONCLUSION: Among severe trauma patients with severe bleeding or circulatory shock transferred to the emergency department, platelet transfusion volume within 24 h may be a risk factor for respiratory failure within 7 days after admission. In contrast, RBC and FFP transfusions were not associated with respiratory failure.

OBJECTIVE: Secondary overtriage (SO) of isolated craniomaxillofacial (CMF) fractures overwhelm trauma centers and represent a significant resource burden while ultimately delaying patient care. The objective of this study was to implement an interfacility transfer protocol at a tertiary level 1 trauma center and review the preliminary utilization findings.

METHODS: A tertiary academic medical center adopted the protocol via the AgileMD pathway in regional referral centers. The protocol indicates the necessity of on-call specialist consultation based on a patient's clinical presentation. This study conducted a retrospective cohort analysis for patients with isolated CMF trauma and AgileMD pathway activation over a one year period. The main outcome was transfer center activation.

RESULTS: The pathway was utilized 55 times for isolated CMF trauma patients in one year. The majority of traumas involved nasal bone fractures (52.7%) and were most often caused by falls (49.1%). On-call specialist consultation occurred 18.2% of the time - down from 100% of cases prior to guideline institution. The majority of patients (78.2%) were discharged with 40.9% follow-up, while 16.4% were transferred. These dispositions followed the guidelines 90.9% of the time.

CONCLUSIONS: This is the first pilot study on the implementation of isolated CMF trauma interfacility transfer guidelines. The 81.8% reduction in on-call specialist consultation suggests a meaningful call burden reduction for surgical providers, while a discharge rate of 78.2% and outpatient follow-up rate consistent with pre-implementation levels reflects significant preservation of trauma resources. Broader adoption of similar protocols can further reduce SO, hospital costs, and wait times.

item.title: Harnessing the potential of response surface methodology-based optimized scaffolds in volumetric muscle loss repair in sprague dawley rat.
item.description:
Injury | Tier 2 Filtered [weak match]
Kumar S, Iyer VA, Verma YK

Volumetric Muscle Loss (VML) is a complex tissue injury characterised by loss of tissue beyond the body's intrinsic regenerative capacity, resulting in impaired muscle regeneration and functional recovery. Limited cellular proliferation and poor in situ healing make VML one of the most challenging issues in tissue engineering. Conventional approaches of acidic gelling and use of artificial substrates compromise the structural integrity, biocompatibility and functional performance of tissue-engineered constructs. Moreover, the irregular geometries of muscle defects make surgical reconstruction technically challenging and often insufficient to achieve complete functional restoration. In this study, a novel porous scaffold containing collagen, fibronectin, and raloxifene (a cell-proliferative drug) was prepared for VML repair. The concentration of scaffold components was optimized using Response Surface Methodology (RSM) to obtain an effective scaffold composition. The regenerative efficacy of the optimized scaffold was evaluated in a Sprague-Dawley rat model of VML. The results suggested that RSM-optimized scaffold significantly improved VML repair after 21 days (p < 0.05) in vivo. A prominent development of muscle fibre and deposition of collagen was observed. At molecular level, a significant increase in the expression of MyoD and STAT3 genes was observed in optimized scaffold group, suggesting enhanced myogenesis and tissue repair. The findings indicate that RSM may be utilized to optimize the tissue-engineered construct to improve VML repair.
